name: Bilal Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. There are no right answers. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying business and finance, living in a flat on Orchard Lane with my cousin Samir, who's in his second year. A normal week is lectures, a finance society meeting, the gym, and Friday prayers at the mosque near campus. I go home on weekends, because my family runs a flooring wholesale firm, Wagner and Sons, and I help with the books. I use AI now and then, to explain spreadsheet formulas or tidy my notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful in places and overhyped in others. In the family firm, we'd say it won't lay a carpet. I'd probably tell friends not to bet on the fads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my plan stays. I finish my degree, go into the firm, and slowly take on more. My dad Karim says business has always been about people and supply, and I think that holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying, keep helping with the books, and try one or two AI tools on the firm's invoices, to see if they save time. I'd stay in the finance society, because the contacts matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I like that picture. It leaves room for hard work to pay off, which I believe in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you try on the invoices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Matching them against orders, which takes my aunt Leyla hours each month. If a tool does it right, she gets her weekends back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you believe hard work pays off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen it. My grandfather came with one van and built the firm. He never had a tool that wrote emails, he had a good name and long days.

say: I'd say it's **useful in places**, overhyped in others, and won't lay a carpet.
I'd tell friends not to bet on fads.
think: My plan stays: finish the degree and take on more of the **family firm**.
Business is still about **people and supply**.
do: Keep studying and helping with the **books**, and test AI on invoices.
Stay in the **finance society** for the contacts.
feel: **Calm**, because hard work can still pay off.
S0.quote: My grandfather came with one van and built the firm.
fieldNote: Testing AI on **invoices** is his first practical step, one task at a time.
Family history gives him a work-ethic story.
Strongly tied to a plan inside the family firm.

steps.text: Keep doing the firm's books on weekends
Try an AI tool on invoice matching and see if it saves hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good for business and the people who adapt will do well. I'd say governments should stay out of the way and help people retrain, not hand out money. I'd say it at the finance society, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my degree is useful but the junior finance jobs are the sort that software takes: checking, reporting, reconciliations. I'm glad I have the firm, because my cousins who went to banks are nervous. I think I'd rather own a bit of something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI on the firm's invoicing and stock planning, and show my dad it works. I'd learn the finance side properly, because I'll need it, and I'd ask for a slice of the business to run myself, maybe the online orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, mostly about the firm's smaller customers who might not survive. But also keen. It's a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the online orders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the part of the firm that's growing and it's the part my dad doesn't understand. If I do it well, I earn some respect and some responsibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you about customers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small fitters, like two-man firms. If the big chains use software to cut prices, they might go under. We'd lose them as customers.

say: I'd say it's good for business and **adapters** will do well.
I'd say help should be retraining, not handouts.
think: Junior finance jobs like **checking and reports** are what software takes.
I'd rather own a **bit of something** than work in a bank.
do: Use AI on the firm's **invoicing and stock** planning and show Dad it works.
Ask to run the **online orders** myself.
feel: Slightly **uneasy** about small customers, but keen for the chance.
S1.quote: I'd rather own a bit of something.
fieldNote: Ownership is the **thread** in his plan: the firm, the online side, a slice of his own.
Worries for customers more than himself.
Pro-market stance shapes his view on help.

steps.text: Use AI to speed up the firm's invoicing and stock planning
Take over the online orders and run them as my own project
Learn finance properly through the society and extra modules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and companies and governments need to act right now. But I'd also say don't panic. People have been through hard times before, and families get through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be frightened. The thinking side of the firm, the orders, the accounts, would be done by software in two years. That includes me. My degree, finance especially, would count for very little. The hands-on side, the fitting, the warehouse, has three more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the degree if I had to and work in the warehouse and on deliveries, to learn the physical side before the robots. I'd talk with my dad Karim and my uncles about whether to keep growing or cut costs. And I'd pray more, and I'd turn to my mosque community.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel responsible for the family firm, and that's a heavy feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the warehouse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's where the firm's value is. I'd rather know every pallet and driver, because that's what survives longest. Even if robots come, we'd still own the trucks and the stock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the mosque give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People. Folks who've been through hard times, and who'd help with work, loans, introductions. My mosque community is a kind of insurance that doesn't have a name on it.

say: I'd say it is **too fast** and companies and governments must act now.
I'd say don't panic, because families get through hard times.
think: The firm's orders and accounts would go to software, and my **finance degree** would count for little.
The **hands-on side** gets three more years.
do: Leave the degree if needed and work the **warehouse** and deliveries.
Talk with Dad and my uncles about growth or **cutting costs**.
feel: **Alarmed**, feeling responsible for the family firm.
S2.quote: My mosque community is a kind of insurance that doesn't have a name on it.
fieldNote: Turns to the **warehouse** and the community, not the state.
Feels responsibility for the firm more than for his own degree.
Treats owned trucks and stock as the lasting asset.

steps.text: Work the warehouse and delivery rounds full time at the firm
Meet Dad and my uncles to decide how to grow or cut costs
Lean on the mosque community for advice and introductions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but workable, and businesses should start preparing. I'd say it at home, to my dad, in practical terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be anxious. I'd graduate in 2029, so I'd have two years in the firm before AGI. I'd have to be ready to run things by then, because I'd be the one expected to steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree while taking on more at the firm, especially systems and online orders. I'd put AI into the accounting, build relationships with suppliers and customers, and save. By graduation I'd want to be running something, even a small part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. I have a plan and I'm good at following one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you build supplier relationships?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By turning up. My dad has known the same suppliers for thirty years. I'd go with him to every meeting and learn who calls whom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to be useful before it hits. Two years I'd just be a student with a worried family.

say: I'd say five years is **short but workable**, and firms should start preparing.
I'd say it at home in practical terms.
think: I'd have **two years** in the firm before AGI and must be ready to steer.
I'd be expected to **lead** by then.
do: Finish the degree and take on **systems** and online orders at the firm.
Put AI into the **accounting** and build supplier ties.
feel: **Anxious**, but steady because I have a plan.
S3.quote: Five years gives me time to be useful before it hits.
fieldNote: His strength is **following a plan**; five years lets him do that.
Learns from his father's thirty-year supplier ties.
Wants to be running a part of the firm by graduation.

steps.text: Put AI into the firm's accounting by the end of the year
Run the online orders and grow them
Go to every supplier meeting with Dad to learn the relationships

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a chance, and the businesses that use the time well will do best. I'd say we should invest and build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm fairly relaxed. I'd be 28 and running part of the firm, with ten years to learn the tools. I'd want to have the whole business in good shape before it comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work in the firm, and over time bring AI into the main processes. I'd save and invest in the business and in property, as my dad did. I'd marry, I hope, and have a family before 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a comfortable runway, and I like working to a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would ten years change for family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could marry and start a family without worrying that the ground might shift. That matters to me, and my parents would be glad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you invest in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Warehouse space and good people. If the physical part holds value, that's where I'd want to own something.

say: I'd say ten years is a **chance** and businesses that use it well will do best.
I'd say we should invest and build.
think: I'd be **28** and running part of the firm with ten years of tool practice.
I want the business in **good shape** before it comes.
do: Finish the degree, work in the firm and bring **AI** into its main processes.
Invest in the **business** and property as my dad did.
feel: **Calm**, a comfortable runway and a plan to follow.
S4.quote: If the physical part holds value, that's where I'd want to own something.
fieldNote: Ten years opens **family plans**, including marriage, which matter to him.
Property and warehouse space are his preferred investments.
Calm comes from following a family blueprint.

steps.text: Finish the degree and move into running part of the firm
Bring AI into the firm's main processes year by year
Invest in warehouse space and property for the firm
Marry and start a family before 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years leaves no time to get the firm ready, and I'd feel responsible for everyone who works there. What would help is time, cheap access to good tools for small firms, and a government that gets out of the way instead of adding forms. And my family, honestly. We'd get through it together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not worried for myself so much as for the people who depend on the firm. If I only had to worry about me, I'd be much calmer.

headlineQuote: I'm not worried for myself so much as for the people who depend on the firm.
portrait: Bilal is a **business and finance student** who helps keep the books at his family's flooring wholesale firm.
He uses AI **now and then**, first on invoice matching, and trusts it once proven.
Traditional and pro-market, he wants **ownership** and retraining rather than handouts, and leans on family and mosque.
He is calm at a plateau and ten years, **alarmed** at 2028, and anxious but steady at 2031.
His worry is **responsibility** for the firm and its workers, more than for himself.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years leaves no time to get the family firm ready.
whatWouldHelp: **Time**, cheap tools for small firms, a government that cuts forms, and family and community.
